Promoting Electric Propulsion for Small Watercraft
SeaRam-1 - Unmanned
Prepared for:
Mentor – Mike Briscoe and the American Society of Naval Engineers
Sponsor Organization – Office of Naval Research
By:
Matt Savell, Andres Calvetty, Alyson Bonsu, Rey Vasquez
Under the supervision of
Associate Professor, Department of Mechanical and Nuclear Engineering:
Hong Zhao
With Assistance From: The VCU Makers Studio and Garage
March 25, 2025 Background

The continuously evolving global trends in technology define our daily lives, along with the ones who are tasked to defend
them. As such, public and private U.S. defense stakeholders have taken key observations from past and current conflicts to create
solutions that will set the pace for what is needed to secure the future. To meet the needs of tomorrow’s challenges, the Office of
Naval Research (ONR) in partnership with the American Society of Naval Engineers (ASNE) have created the Promoting
Electric Propulsion (PEP) competition.
 While PEP is a constructed learning opportunity and friendly competition, there are greater challenges it seeks to address.
These include cost-effective, modular, scalable, systems for naval technology. The U.S. military in particular is pivoting to
highly efficient systems that maximize funding and size, partially in the unmanned realm. Numerous lessons learned from past
and present conflicts, including Ukraine and Russia, have driven this doctrinal refocusing to be ready for threats on the horizon
[1]. The focus on electric based propulsion also has environmental significance through the reduction of pollution sourced from
vehicles’ emissions can significantly advance efforts to improve our planet's health and economic benefits from the electric sector
and job creation. Electric power is one of the leading capabilities being researched to achieve this [2]. Accordingly, the U.S. The
Navy, among other military branches, is attempting to set the pace through climate-based commitments [3].
 Given this reality the VCU PEP team has taken these challenges into consideration when designing the university's second
entry into the competition. From the onset, a balance of performance, reliability, and efficiency were set as pillars of the team’s
watercraft. Using the hull passed down from the previous team allowed for greater work to be done on other systems while
reducing the uncertainty of creating a hull without experience or sufficient knowledge. The use of a non-custom hull also proves
that our design can be placed into many other hulls with minimal redesign. The power supply of Li-Po batteries ensures a
scalable electric energy source that is readily available and proven to work. The drive-train for the boat has been designed to
maximize efficiency while meeting the demands of a significant payload and high speed maneuvering that is critical in many
modern naval applications. Special attention has been given to this section as the previous year’s team had a competition-ending
failure in this regard. The team’s electrical subsystems are based in reliable integration and safety to ensure all components work
with each other as seamlessly as possible to maximize performance and reduring danger to the users. The payload will be held
by a custom housing unit that can be easily adjusted to allow for mission-based modularity. The payload carriage system and
other custom parts such a battery trays, and turn fins highlight originality of the team and their capability to create high quality
solutions from the ground up.
Design & Analysis
Drivetrain Design
 The motors serve as the core components of the drivetrain. The current design utilizes two 500 kV, 6-pole brushless motors
(SSS 56123-V2 KV500) Figure 1 to power and propel the craft. The combination of a higher pole count and a 500 kV rating
provides increased torque, which is critical for accelerating the vehicle while carrying a payload between 30–60 lbs. The
dual-motor configuration enhances acceleration and top speed, improves overall stability, and introduces redundancy in case of
motor failure. In PEP 2024, a single 53100 1450 kV 8-pole brushless motor was used. For the 2025 iteration, a thrust analysis
was conducted using this motor, which yielded approximately 16 lbs of thrust at full throttle. The resulting thrust-to-weight ratio,
accounting for a 30 lb payload, was calculated to be 0.34. Given that the desired thrust-to-weight ratio was determined to be
between 0.6 and 1.0, the team explored alternative propulsion systems. Following consultation with industry experts and internal
analysis, a dual-motor system utilizing two 500 kV, 6-pole brushless motors was selected to balance torque and speed. The
decision was validated through a thrust calculation based on The Propeller Handbook by Dave Gerr. Key assumptions in the
analysis included a target speed of 60 mph (used as a competitive benchmark), a drivetrain and propeller efficiency of 0.5 (to represent worst-case performance), a hull wake drag coefficient of 0.95, and a motor power output of 15,000 W. The analysis

produced a calculated thrust of 66.25 lbs per motor, or 132.5 lbs total for the dual system. This results in a thrust-to-weight ratio
of 1.12, slightly above the target range but acceptable due to the conservative nature of the assumptions and minor additional
losses from the drive cable and mechanical friction.
Figure 1: Twin SSS 56123-V2 KV500 Motors Mounted Figure 2: Thrust - Weight Calculations
 The rudder assembly plays a critical role in the drivetrain system. The current design features a dual-strut rudder assembly
Figure 2, which increases the total surface area in the water. This enhancement improves directional stability and control,
particularly during high-speed runs and sharp turns. In PEP 2024, a single stinger rudder assembly was used. For PEP 2025, due
to the increased payload of 30–60 lbs, the design was upgraded to a dual-strut rudder system to maintain performance and
prevent washout during aggressive maneuvers. This configuration includes adjustable strut mounts for the drive cable, enabling
fine-tuning of motor angle for improved efficiency. Each rudder is also equipped with two water pickups, providing active
cooling to both ESCs and motors, which helps maintain consistent thermal management across the system. The drive cable is a
vital component in transmitting motor power efficiently. The current design uses two ¼ inch Hughey Drive Cables, chosen for
their ability to resist twisting under high torque. The increased diameter ensures consistent power delivery and reduces the risk of
failure under load. In the 2024 setup, a smaller drive cable was used, which led to a catastrophic failure during competition
Figure 3. As a result, the design was upgraded to a more robust ¼ in drive cable for 2025. The Hughey cable offers superior
strength and durability, significantly lowering the likelihood of mechanical failure and ensuring reliable operation under high
torque conditions. Figure 3: Failure from PEP 2024

The propeller, or prop, offers some of the most complexity and impact when it comes to drivetrain design and choice. Based
on the team’s research two categories of propeller variables yield the most influence while also being the most customizable.
These categories are propeller diameter and pitch or the theoretical distance a propeller would move forward in one revolution if
it were moving through a solid medium [4]. Propeller design from scratch is a highly cumbersome task, however, a large number
of options exist, as seen in Figure 4 that allow the team to sift through and optimize based on hull and drivetrain characteristics
The first prop variable that was optimized was the diameter. Using the calculations in Figure 5, an idealized size range was
found by incorporating the power needed based on hull length. To find the ideal pitch the calculations in Figure 6 were
performed. The equation used a variable boat speed, motor gear ratio (set as 1 since the team’s design is direct), engine rotation,
an assumed slip percentage (a type of pitch inefficiency), and a conversion constant. The calculation was repeated for an ideal no
slip condition as well an assumed slip condition. All results were averaged across a set of low to high speeds to achieve the most
balanced pitch for all possible conditions. Thus, two propeller designs were chosen from over a hundred options, one with the
original diameter (65mm), and a second based on the ideal pitch (4 in.) and an incrementally increased diameter (71mm) to
reduce cavitation while not interfering with the dual motor/propeller setup.
Figure 4: Section of Supplier’s Propeller Chart Figure 5: Propeller Diameter Calculation Figure 6: Propeller Pitch Calculations

Electrical and Power System Design
 The RC boat’s original electrical system, based on a previous team’s design, had inefficiencies in weight distribution and
power management. It used ten batteries, adding excessive mass without proportional performance gains, and lacked adequate
circuit protection. To improve efficiency while meeting competition constraints, the new design optimizes power use, reduces
weight, and enhances safety. The battery count was reduced to eight, maintaining power output while lowering weight. A fuse
box and a waterproof 300A circuit breaker were added for protection. The improved system features eight 10,000 mAh, 6S-25C,
22.2V batteries in parallel, keeping voltage under the 55V limit. The propulsion system includes kV500 motors with neodymium
magnets, delivering up to 15,800W. The OM-300 AHV 300A RC Boat ESC ensures efficient motor control, while 6 AWG and 8
AWG wiring with XT90 and EC8 connectors handle high currents. For control, a Spektrum DX6C transmitter and SR515
receiver provide precise maneuverability. To reduce receiver load, hydraulic pumps (1000 cc/min flow rate) use an external
battery. These improvements enhance power management, reliability, and compliance with performance and safety requirements.
Payload Design
 Research on payload systems for boats turned up minimal existing designs that were applicable. Full size systems for large
vessels were not feasible for the team’s boat size of 84 inches. For small model and RC boats, the most extensive systems simply
put weight on top of the hull meaning a fully original design was needed for the year’s weight requirements. Some military
applications exist but their specifics are not open source. To be in line with the direction of modern naval systems’ priority of
scalability and modularity, the payload system for the team’s boat focuses on flexible placement of multiple weights, secure lock
down during maneuvers, and an adaptable core set of parts that can be adjusted as needed. One of the largest challenges of the
payload system was overcoming the angled shape of our V-hull design. A method of cut and angled 2x4 wood beams was chosen
to level each side of the boat and create a stable foundation. This allowed for aluminum rails to be mounted giving way to the
use of heavy-duty locking rail carriages. Four carriages are used to create balanced and stable linear movement for each payload
while being able to lock in place when necessary. Multiple iterations of 3D printed risers are used to overcome spacing and
clearance issues such as with the locking mechanism of the carriage and the main drivetrain and battery elements in the center of
the boat. For the actual payload, 30lb ruck weights are used as they are an optional combination of a small form factor without
movement from a medium such as sandbags. Each weight is secured to the rest of the design through ¾ inch plywood, 3D
printed supports, ¼ inch bolts, and quick release nuts to ensure the payload’s stability when the boat is in motion. An overview
of the design is shown in Figure 7. Notably, the overall design permits two of the described systems giving the team the
flexibility to choose between carrying 30lbs or 60lbs. Figure 7: Payload System Overview

Hydromatic Addition Design
 Turn fins, most commonly found on miniature race boats, are fixed past the transom of the craft to provide additional surface area
to create a counter-force when it makes turns. Many varying versions of turn fins exist, but few offer a size that the team deemed
optimal through a general observation of hull length to turn fin length ratios of about 1:11. To accommodate, the team 3D modeled
multiple sets of common turn fins in addition to creating an original design based on fish and rocket fins. The design combines the
low aspect and taper ratios (1:1.7) found in rocket fins and shark fins (sharks are optimal for comparison as they are more stiff than
other fish, resembling a boat better), with the higher ratios (1:7) found in wind sails. This shape mimics dorsal fins found in what
research has shown to be faster fish as well as the “shark fin” of F1 race cars of the past. To mount the turn fins a custom design
was created to permit the best range of motion of adjusting the fins’ angle. The trim tab design utilizes locking hinges that can be
set at any angle from 0 to 180 degrees. Sizing was determined by recommendations of one inch of span per foot of hull length.
Figure 8: Hydrodynamic Addition Overview
Custom Mounting Designs
  A custom mount was designed to secure the stuffing tubes and house the circuit breakers Figure 9. This setup was chosen to

maximize internal space while also providing easy access to the circuit breakers in case they trip during operation. Additionally,
the mount keeps the stuffing tubes firmly in place, helping to minimize vibration and unwanted movement while the craft is
running.
Figure 9: Custom Mount for Drive Cables and ESC’s
 To help optimize the boat weight and improve efficiency of the electrical system, custom battery mounts were modelled using
SOLIDWORKS then 3D printed, as shown in Figure 10. Two mounts were printed, each able to hold up to four batteries. Each
battery will be held in a separate slot and secured by a custom harness utilizing a velcro strip connected to a scaled belt buckle, as
shown in Figure 11. This harness system allows for quick installation and removal of each battery, which could be critical for
preserving integrity of various components or systems inside the boat. One slot in each set is angled and has a smaller slot
embossed into the angled end, allowing for the other security system to activate. This system is a spring lock mechanism located
inside the angled end of the battery slot base, as shown in Figure 12. A spring block connected to an external grip will be pushed
into the angled slot by two internal springs, which can be compressed via the external grip when removal is desired. Each set of
slots will be connected to a wood locking block underneath, which will link each set of four slots and act as a secondary form of
security simultaneously.

 Figure 10: Overview of Battery Mount. Figure 11: Belt Buckle/Strip Harness System.
Figure 12: Spring Lock Mechanism. Hull

To provide extra visualization and a foundation for expected boat performance, hydrodynamic and vector analysis was
conducted. The hydrodynamic analysis of the boat hull was conducted first to visualize the benefit of hull strakes and gain a basic
understanding of what performance to expect at peak operational condition. A simplified version of the boat model was recreated
with and without strakes while water conditions were studied at the site of operation, shown in Figure 13 and 14. Preliminary
hydrodynamic diffraction was conducted before hydrodynamic responses were studied. The frequency of the wave movement
while moving was adjusted alongside the water speed to help visualize how the boat will react to the expected conditions. The
results of this hydrodynamic analysis were significant in estimating the performance of the boat when including the weight of the
payload alongside the internals. The hull studied without strakes was shown to drift to one side, with a longer simulation resulting
in the boat tipping. The hull with strakes included showed much better performance stability wise, with minimal drifting that
could easily be accounted for with trim settings. To further visualize and study the boat’s performance under operational
conditions, a multi-phase flow vector analysis was conducted. The analysis was conducted with the hull with strakes included
utilized in the previous analysis at the peak expected operational speed. The results of the simulation yielded promising results,
with a wake expected to pass around but not over the boat, which is expected to improve as planning is achieved. The vector field
of the expected wake is shown in Figure 15. The wake is also expected to keep the propeller submerged despite the amount of
water displaced, further contributing to the planning potential. Utilizing the built in characteristics calculator in ANSYS Fluent
post alongside material and weight data, the expected drag force was able to be determined, which is around 40 lb (177 N) when
travelling at 48 mph.

 Figure 13: Simplified Hull w/o Strakes Figure 14: Simplified Hull With Strakes
Figure 15: Vector Field of Multi-Phase Flow Analysis
Drivetrain Analysis
 The team plotted the thrust output of the motors across various speeds Figure 16 to better understand their performance
characteristics under different operating conditions. This visualization provides a clear representation of how thrust varies with
speed, enabling identification of the motor’s efficiency range and highlighting the speeds at which performance peaks or begins to taper off. By analyzing this data, the team was able to determine the optimal throttle settings that balance power consumption

with propulsion efficiency—particularly important when operating under payload conditions between 30–60 lbs. The resulting
thrust curve also informed decisions regarding battery selection and propeller choice, ensuring that the drivetrain operates within
its most effective range. Additionally, having access to this data allows for the simulation of different mission profiles and
provides insight into how the system will respond in real-world conditions, such as accelerating out of turns or maintaining high
speeds during straight-line sprints. Ultimately, this analysis is crucial for fine-tuning the craft to optimize both performance and
reliability.

Figure 16: Thrust - Speed Data Figure 17: Thrust - Speed Graph
Electrical and Power System Analysis
 The redesigned electrical and power system significantly enhances the RC boat’s performance, efficiency, and reliability while
meeting all competition constraints. One of the most important improvements was the optimization of the battery configuration.
By reducing the battery count from ten to eight, the system achieves a more efficient power-to-weight ratio without
compromising performance. This adjustment lowers the overall mass of the boat, improving buoyancy and maneuverability while
maintaining sufficient power output. The parallel battery configuration ensures consistent voltage levels, providing stable power
delivery to the propulsion and auxiliary systems. A key consideration in the design was circuit protection. The inclusion of a
waterproof 300A circuit breaker and fuse box mitigates the risk of electrical failures, safeguarding both the components and
overall system integrity. This protection is essential given the high current demands of the propulsion system, which operates at
peak loads nearing 15,800W. Without adequate circuit protection, excessive current draw could lead to overheating, component
damage, or system shutdowns, all of which could jeopardize the boat’s performance during the competition. The selection of the
kV500 motors and OM-300 AHV, 300A ESC was based on a balance between power efficiency and control precision. The
motors, equipped with neodymium magnets, offer high torque and energy efficiency, enabling the boat to maintain optimal thrust
without unnecessary power losses. The ESC further enhances performance by regulating motor speed and ensuring smooth
acceleration and deceleration, critical for maintaining control over the boat during the 2-mile course. The use of 6 AWG and 8
AWG wiring minimizes resistive losses, preventing voltage drops that could otherwise impact motor efficiency and system
stability. Another critical improvement was the separation of the hydraulic pumps from the main power system by assigning
them an external battery source. This prevents excessive current draw from interfering with the propulsion system, reducing the
risk of power fluctuations that could impair maneuverability. The integration of the Spektrum DX6C transmitter and SR515
receiver provides precise control, allowing for accurate adjustments to steering and throttle inputs. These enhancements
collectively ensure the RC boat operates efficiently while maintaining the necessary power levels for propulsion and auxiliary
functions. To provide a clear representation of the electrical layout, a schematic diagram of the system is included below, Figures 18 and 19. This schematic illustrates the connections between the batteries, circuit protection elements, ESC, motors,

hydraulic pumps, and control components. Key aspects highlighted in the diagram include: Power Distribution, Circuit
Protection, Motor & ESC Connections, Control System.

Figure 18: Parallel Battery Schematic Figure 19: Main Electronic component Section
Overall, the redesigned electrical and power system successfully addresses the inefficiencies of the previous
iteration by optimizing power distribution, implementing robust circuit protection, and improving energy efficiency. These
improvements contribute to a more reliable and high-performing vessel capable of completing the 2-mile course within the
required 55-minute time frame while adhering to all competition constraints.
Payload Analysis
 Given the need for reliability within the payload system an simulation based analysis of various the key structural components
was done in SolidWorks. Using a full 3D render allowed the team to pinpoint the most crucial elements of the design within a
greater visual context. The following simulations were completed by reducing a 30lb distributed load along the top surface:
deformation analysis, stress analysis, strain analysis, and a factor of safety (FOS) analysis shown in Figure 20. Since the 3D
model used to simulate the payload system was a 1:1 working digital version of what would become the actual system, accurate
material properties were compiled into the software to allow each component to be realistically depicted under load. The results
of the simulation yield a deformation range of 3.9x10 to 1.1x inches with the max occurring at the center of the plywood −32 10−4
support. The stress ranged from 1.2x10 to 8.6x psi with a section of the aluminum rails under most force per area. The −3 101
strain results ranged from 3.9x10 to 1.7x with the highest amounts occurring at the edges of the large 3D printed risers. −9 10−5
To better contextualize these results the FOS results offer the most insight. With a range of 4.6x10 to 8.8x , most of the 1
106
system lay within the lower end of the FOS, however, this value is still significantly large and permitted the team to move
forward with the design with greater confidence. Figure 20: Structural Analysis via Solidworks

Propeller Analysis
 To visualize and confirm the performance improvements of larger propellers, simulation utilizing ANSYS Fluent was
conducted. The study was dedicated to comparing the set of 2.5 inch diameter propellers with a 3.5 inch pitch to an upgraded 2.7
inch diameter set of propellers with a 4.32 inch pitch. The main point of focus for each simulation was the amount of thrust and
torque each propeller can output. Pressure contours and water velocity vector fields were also synthesized for supporting
analysis. These characteristics were determined to be the most relevant points of study due to their potential impact on the boat
throughout operation. Both propellers will experience 11,000 RPM at 40 mph to simulate close to maximum expected operational
conditions, with all movement other than rotation on the Z axis locked. Due to the focus on geometry, material properties will not
be relevant throughout this study despite being accurately assigned. Initial research of the impact of an increased diameter and
pitch showed that the increased diameter will have a greater thrust and torque but experience greater drag, while the increased
pitch would allow for a higher top speed at the cost of a slower acceleration. The results of the study yielded promising
results, with the 2.7 in diameter propeller demonstrating an average thrust of around 875 N (~196 lbf) after achieving stable
operation 1 second after startup, both of which are shown on Figure 21. The 2.7 in propeller achieved an average torque of
around 12 Nm (~106 in-lb), shown in Figure 22. The 2.5 in propeller yielded expected results, with an average thrust of around
462.5 N (~104 lbf) after reaching stability half a second after startup, as shown in Figure 23. The 2.5 in propeller achieved an
average torque of around 8 Nm (~70 in-lb) after reaching stability in a similar time frame to the thrust graph as shown in Figure
24. Each force and torque graph pair share a very similar curve due to the thrust and torque applied being proportional to each
other. These simulations confirm the validity of the initial research, as the 2.7 in propeller had greater amount of thrust and torque
compared to the 2.5 in propeller while experiencing a slower acceleration to stability by half a second. Water velocity vector
profiles and pressure contours were also synthesized for study. Figures 25 and 26 show the face and back pressure contours for
the 2.5 in propeller, with the back side of the propeller being of note due to the presence of multiple smaller low pressure zones
having a high potential to cause cavitation during physical operation. Figures 27 and 28 show the face and back pressure
contours for the 2.7 in propeller, which show more consistent pressure zones. These pressure zones being more consistent
translates to less cavitation at the operational RPM, solidifying the 2.7 in diameter propeller as beneficial and necessary for
optimal operation. Figures 29 and 30 show the water velocity vector profiles for the 2.5 and 2.7 inch propellers respectively. The
water movement around the 2.5 in propeller is faster in comparison to the 2.7 in propeller, which confirms that a smaller diameter
propeller will be faster and produce less drag than a larger diameter propeller, but will reduce the amount of torque output.

Figure 21: 2.7 in Diameter Propeller Thrust Graph Figure 22: 2.7 in Diameter Propeller Torque Graph
Figure 23: 2.5 in Diameter Propeller Thrust Graph Figure 24: 2.5 in Diameter Propeller Torque Graph
 Figure 25: face side pressure contour of 2.5 in Prop Figure 26: back side pressure contour of 2.5 in Prop

 Figure 27: face side pressure contour of 2.7 in Prop Figure 28: back side pressure contour of 2.7 in Prop Figure 29: Water Velocity Vector Field of 2.5 in Propeller Figure 30: Water Velocity Vector Field of 2.7 in Propeller

Build & Fabrication
Drivetrain
 The majority of the build and fabrication phase of this project was focused on the drivetrain. The first step was mounting the
rudder, as its position determined the alignment and fitment of the remaining components. Next, the team fiberglassed wood
stringers into the hull, providing a rigid and secure base for all components without needing to drill directly into the boat itself.
Following that, the motors were mounted to the stingers using custom CNC-machined aluminum mounts. They were set at a
5-degree downward angle to help reduce cavitation and ensure efficient power transmission Figure 1. We then bent and installed
the stuffing tubes using our custom mount. The tubes were shaped in an S-curve to help reduce vibration from the flexible drive
shaft. Final steps included installing Teflon washers to minimize friction between the struts and props. The drive cables were
greased, inserted through the stuffing tubes, and secured to the motors. Lastly, the props were attached and locked in place using
nylon locking nuts.
Electrical and Power System
 During the building and fabrication of the unmanned boat, the placement of electronic components was carefully determined
after implementing the drivetrain, which occupied a significant amount of space near the transom. With the batteries positioned at
the nose of the boat to aid in weight distribution, the remaining electronics had to be rearranged to fit efficiently within the
available space. As a result, the ESC was positioned directly underneath the motor, while the circuit breaker was mounted on
custom-made stuffing tube mounts. These placement decisions were influenced by several critical factors, including balance, heat
dissipation, and accessibility for maintenance. Placing the ESC under the motor minimized wiring complexity by reducing the
length of connections between key components, which helped optimize power delivery and system efficiency. Additionally, this
location provided adequate airflow to help dissipate heat generated during operation, preventing potential overheating issues. The
circuit breaker was strategically mounted on the stuffing tube mounts to ensure it remained secure while also being easily
accessible for maintenance and troubleshooting. This placement facilitated quick power isolation if needed, enhancing both
safety and ease of operation. Overall, these design choices allowed for an efficient, well-organized layout that balanced
performance, thermal management, and serviceability within the spatial constraints of the vessel. Payload

The foundation of the payload system hindered upon the size, space, and geometry of the hull. Internal measurements were
taken to set a baseline for design and fabrication. Most importantly, each side of the hull was measured which produced unique
angles due. While only minimally different with the left side being 15 degrees and the right being 18 degrees, accounting for this
difference was critical for the rest of the design. This was displayed most critically in the wood supports that used 2x4 studs cut
using a table saw into right triangles with each of aforementioned angles thus leveling each side. The supports were then
fiberglassed into the hull to create a high-strength base. The even surface created by the supports allows the rail system to
operate as smoothly as possible. Said rail system is mounted using M5 bolts/screws/nuts. It was decided to have the screws
come from the bottom of the wood support to prevent them from being easily ripped out. This decision required countersunk
holes to keep the critical angle alignment. Additionally, the first set of 3D printed risers were created to allow the rails to sit
higher above the wood allowing the locking mechanism of the rail carriage to operate. The second set of risers were made larger
and more robust to copacetically fit with the rail carriages while supporting the load and providing clearance above the drivetrain
and electrical systems. M4 screws/nuts were used to fix these items together. The main ¾ inch plywood support was cut to the
largest size that could fit inside the access point of the hull to maximize the distribution of the load. Mounting holes were then
drilled along a calculated pattern that permitted the plywood to be fixed to the larger rise supports. Additional supports for the
payload were 3D printed to lock the ruck weight in place and prevent displacements through multiple degrees of motion. These
elements were then assembled with ¼ inch bolts/nuts to ensure strength and stability. A ¼ inch plywood sheet was then used as a
lid with the same hole pattern. The design intentionally let the bolts show above the lit which permits the use of specially quick
release, push-button ¼ inch nuts to be used for locking the weight in.
Custom Mounting
 Design of the custom battery mount needed to take the boat stringers and boat geometry into account, which was done through
measurements taken before design was initiated. The critical measurements taken were the distance between the stringers (insert
here) and an internal angle of 20 degrees inside the boat. The first step to assembly was gluing the mounting bases together,
which was done using Weld-On 16 acrylic cement due to the nature of its chemical bond providing unmatched strength. At the
same time, the wood locking base was cut from stock wood and glued together with wood glue. After the bonding time had
passed, the mounting base and wood locking base was tested to confirm correct sizing. The battery slot assemblies were then
assembled as parts were delivered, utilizing a plastic hinge and a velcro strip connected to the belt clip. The clip and harness base
were both secured to each slot with 8 total M4x8 screws. Once the mounting slots and wood locking base are complete, they will
be glued together with a thin coat of a universal adhesive. Before the mounting base is glued onto a wood base inside the boat,
the spring lock system will be assembled with Weld-On 16. Epoxy resin will be used to glue the mounting base to the wood base,
which will then be attached to the boat internally in a similar fashion.
Hydrodynamic Additions
 Turnfins and trimtabs will be 3D printed for testing. An infill of 50% or greater will be used to provide the greatest strength
and reliability. Once the final designs are determined, the turn fins and trimtabs will be CNC machined out of an aluminum alloy
metal. The turn fins and trim tabs will be mounted to the rear of the craft. Mounting holes will be drilled to allow M4 screws to
pass through, and the components will be secured using nylon locking nuts. To ensure a watertight seal and prevent any leaks,
3M marine sealant will be applied around the mounting points during installation. The actual additions will be 3D printed at high
infill percentages for the highest quality results. Testing

A series of tests will be conducted to verify the boat’s seaworthiness, endurance, and overall performance. Testing will take
place at either Swan Lake or Robious Landing Park, both locations provide calm waters and sufficient space for full-capacity
operation. The first test will involve placing the boat in the water to check for leaks and ensure all systems are functioning
correctly, including the motors, ESCs, rudder, and water pumps. A force gauge will be attached to measure thrust at various
throttle levels.The second test will assess the boat’s endurance by verifying it can travel 2 miles without any added payload. The
third and fourth tests will evaluate performance under load: first with a 30-pound payload, then with a 60-pound payload, each
over a 2-mile course. Additional tests will focus on maneuverability and handling to familiarize the team with boat operation and
to identify and address any potential issues prior to competition.
Risk
Drivetrain
 For the motors, the primary risk lies in power consumption. Due to their high-performance nature, they draw significant
power, which could lead to rapid battery drain. To mitigate this, we plan to test various throttle settings and optimize our battery
usage accordingly. Additionally, we aim to implement battery telemetry for real-time voltage monitoring to prevent unexpected
power loss during operation. For the rudder, the main concern is increased drag. Since we are using a dual rudder setup, there is
more surface area in the water, which slightly increases resistance. However, given the high thrust output from the motors, this
additional drag is minimal and considered negligible in terms of overall performance. The risk associated with the drive shaft is
excessive friction and mechanical stress, which could lead to failure. To address this, we will follow a strict maintenance
routine—cleaning and drying the shaft after each use and applying fresh grease before every run to ensure smooth operation and
longevity. For the props, the risk is potential loosening or imbalance during operation. To prevent this, we use nylon locking nuts
to secure the props and inspect them regularly for wear or damage. Ensuring they are properly torqued and balanced helps
maintain efficiency and avoid mechanical issues at high speeds.
Electrical and Power System
 To address the risks associated with the electrical components and power systems, several design strategies and preventative
measures were implemented to enhance the safety, reliability, and performance of the unmanned boat. One of the primary
concerns was heat buildup due to the ESC’s placement directly underneath the motor. To mitigate this, adequate ventilation was
ensured by allowing sufficient airflow around the ESC and motor, enabling natural heat dissipation. Additionally, a heat sink was
installed on the ESC to improve thermal regulation and prevent overheating during extended operation. The circuit breaker’s
location on custom-made stuffing tube mounts initially posed a risk of mechanical stress and vibrations from the drivetrain,
which could lead to unintentional tripping or premature wear. To counter this, vibration-dampening materials were integrated into
the mounting system, reducing excessive movement and preventing accidental breaker trips. The breaker was also strategically
positioned to remain easily accessible for maintenance while being securely fastened to prevent disconnections due to mechanical
strain. Another potential risk was electromagnetic interference (EMI) affecting signal integrity due to the proximity of
high-current components. To resolve this, shielded cables were used for critical wiring, particularly for data and control lines,
while power cables were routed separately to minimize interference. Additionally, secure cable management techniques,
including zip ties and protective tubing, were employed to prevent accidental disconnections, wire fatigue, or damage from
vibrations. By implementing these mitigation strategies, the risks associated with the electrical and power systems were
effectively reduced, ensuring stable performance, reliability, and longevity of the unmanned boat’s electrical components. Payload

The payload presents a number of risks, most prominently from unwanted displacements and structural failure. Having a
movable payload is critical for accessing other elements and testing the optimal position for operation. Since a moveable payload
is so critical for the design, the application of locking rail carriages to fix the payload in place was essential in addressing any
concerns. The carriages are also rated to withstand a large amount of force from pitching, yawing, and rolling motions,
especially when used congruently in multiples. Material selection and geometric design was done in a fashion that combined
desirable traits and distributed loads over larger areas while resisting deformation. The load simulations run helped confirm that
the team adequately addressed any risk related to the loads. As was also mentioned above, 3D printing allowed many elements to
be iterated upon reducing the risk of impeding on other critical components. The strategic use of push-button quick-release nuts
also gives the team a faster way to prepare the payload during the five minutes allowed after the weight-in stage. This reduces
the risk of the team being penalized for a time violation without compromising structural integrity.
Custom Mounting
 The primary risk associated with the battery mounting system is structural failure. Fatigue and stress failure concerns are
present throughout the system but the most critical is fatigue failure in the belt clip. The belt clip system is capable of supporting
the battery when the full weight of the battery is placed on it, but over multiple unlocking and locking cycles the belt clip prongs
will begin to experience plastic deformation, loosening the clip until it could potentially be shaken free or snap from overuse.
This potential failure point Is alleviated by increasing the size of the belt clip system, increasing the yield strength of the prongs
and allowing for longer continued use. Another potential point of failure is stress failure of the wood base holding the mounting
system inside the boat. Due to the weight of the batteries on the mount there is potential for either the wood base to snap, or the
epoxy resin to fail. If time permits, a successful solution would involve creating a vertical support below the base, utilizing the
bottom of the boat to alleviate the stress the wood base would experience.
Hydrodynamic Additions
 The primary risk of the hydrodynamic additions is structural failure. Most pre-made versions of these designs use CNC
technology. This is an option that the current team will keep on the table and pass on to future teams. However, given the current
set of time and monetary constraints, 3D printing offers the most viable solution. As mentioned in the fabrication section, high
infill rates will increase the density of the prints ensuring a more durable construction. Furthermore, a cross-compatible
mounting design for the original trim tabs will be used to allow them to be interchangeable with the procured version, limiting the
risk of unnecessary hull patching. A secondary risk associated with the trim tabs and turn fins is improper alignment or
installation, which can lead to handling instability or inefficient hydrodynamics. If the trim tabs are not correctly leveled, the craft
may experience uneven lift or porpoising at high speeds. Similarly, misaligned turn fins can cause unpredictable turning behavior
or increased drag. To mitigate these risks, precise measurement and alignment will be performed during installation, and all
hardware will be securely fastened using nylon locking nuts and marine sealant to prevent shifting during operation. Regular
inspections will be conducted to ensure components remain tight and properly positioned after each run. Another potential risk is
water leakage through the mounting holes; this will be addressed by applying 3M marine-grade sealant around all screw holes to
maintain watertight integrity.Citations

[1] Two years of War in Ukraine: What the Pentagon has learned - The Washington Post,
https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2024/02/22/ukraine-war-pentagon-lessons-learned/ (accessed Oct. 4, 2024).
[2] EPA, https://www.epa.gov/greenvehicles/electric-vehicle-myths (accessed Oct. 4, 2024).
[3] “Department of the Navy releases Climate action 2030,” United States Navy,
https://www.navy.mil/Press-Office/Press-Releases/display-pressreleases/Article/3041221/department-of-the-navy-releases-climat
e-action-2030/ (accessed Oct. 4, 2024).
[4] “Understanding a Boat’s Propeller Pitch,” Discover Boating. https://www.discoverboating.com/resources/propeller-pitch
[5] D. Gerr, Propeller Handbook: The Complete Reference for Choosing, Installing, and Understanding Boat Propellers.
International Marine Publishing, 1989.

source_lines.text: Promoting Electric Propulsion for Small Watercraft
SeaRam-1 - Unmanned
Prepared for:
Mentor – Mike Briscoe and the American Society of Naval Engineers
Sponsor Organization – Office of Naval Research
By:
Matt Savell, Andres Calvetty, Alyson Bonsu, Rey Vasquez
Under the supervision of
Associate Professor, Department of Mechanical and Nuclear Engineering:
Hong Zhao
With Assistance From: The VCU Makers Studio and Garage
March 25, 2025 Background
The continuously evolving global trends in technology define our daily lives, along with the ones who are tasked to defend
them. As such, public and private U.S. defense stakeholders have taken key observations from past and current conflicts to create
solutions that will set the pace for what is needed to secure the future. To meet the needs of tomorrow’s challenges, the Office of
Naval Research (ONR) in partnership with the American Society of Naval Engineers (ASNE) have created the Promoting
Electric Propulsion (PEP) competition.
While PEP is a constructed learning opportunity and friendly competition, there are greater challenges it seeks to address.
These include cost-effective, modular, scalable, systems for naval technology. The U.S. military in particular is pivoting to
highly efficient systems that maximize funding and size, partially in the unmanned realm. Numerous lessons learned from past
and present conflicts, including Ukraine and Russia, have driven this doctrinal refocusing to be ready for threats on the horizon
[1]. The focus on electric based propulsion also has environmental significance through the reduction of pollution sourced from
vehicles’ emissions can significantly advance efforts to improve our planet's health and economic benefits from the electric sector
and job creation. Electric power is one of the leading capabilities being researched to achieve this [2]. Accordingly, the U.S. The
Navy, among other military branches, is attempting to set the pace through climate-based commitments [3].
Given this reality the VCU PEP team has taken these challenges into consideration when designing the university's second
entry into the competition. From the onset, a balance of performance, reliability, and efficiency were set as pillars of the team’s
watercraft. Using the hull passed down from the previous team allowed for greater work to be done on other systems while
reducing the uncertainty of creating a hull without experience or sufficient knowledge. The use of a non-custom hull also proves
that our design can be placed into many other hulls with minimal redesign. The power supply of Li-Po batteries ensures a
scalable electric energy source that is readily available and proven to work. The drive-train for the boat has been designed to
maximize efficiency while meeting the demands of a significant payload and high speed maneuvering that is critical in many
modern naval applications. Special attention has been given to this section as the previous year’s team had a competition-ending
failure in this regard. The team’s electrical subsystems are based in reliable integration and safety to ensure all components work
with each other as seamlessly as possible to maximize performance and reduring danger to the users. The payload will be held
by a custom housing unit that can be easily adjusted to allow for mission-based modularity. The payload carriage system and
other custom parts such a battery trays, and turn fins highlight originality of the team and their capability to create high quality
solutions from the ground up.
Design & Analysis
Drivetrain Design
The motors serve as the core components of the drivetrain. The current design utilizes two 500 kV, 6-pole brushless motors
(SSS 56123-V2 KV500) Figure 1 to power and propel the craft. The combination of a higher pole count and a 500 kV rating
provides increased torque, which is critical for accelerating the vehicle while carrying a payload between 30–60 lbs. The
dual-motor configuration enhances acceleration and top speed, improves overall stability, and introduces redundancy in case of
motor failure. In PEP 2024, a single 53100 1450 kV 8-pole brushless motor was used. For the 2025 iteration, a thrust analysis
was conducted using this motor, which yielded approximately 16 lbs of thrust at full throttle. The resulting thrust-to-weight ratio,
accounting for a 30 lb payload, was calculated to be 0.34. Given that the desired thrust-to-weight ratio was determined to be
between 0.6 and 1.0, the team explored alternative propulsion systems. Following consultation with industry experts and internal
analysis, a dual-motor system utilizing two 500 kV, 6-pole brushless motors was selected to balance torque and speed. The
decision was validated through a thrust calculation based on The Propeller Handbook by Dave Gerr. Key assumptions in the

analysis included a target speed of 60 mph (used as a competitive benchmark), a drivetrain and propeller efficiency of 0.5 (to represent worst-case performance), a hull wake drag coefficient of 0.95, and a motor power output of 15,000 W. The analysis
produced a calculated thrust of 66.25 lbs per motor, or 132.5 lbs total for the dual system. This results in a thrust-to-weight ratio
of 1.12, slightly above the target range but acceptable due to the conservative nature of the assumptions and minor additional
losses from the drive cable and mechanical friction.
Figure 1: Twin SSS 56123-V2 KV500 Motors Mounted Figure 2: Thrust - Weight Calculations
The rudder assembly plays a critical role in the drivetrain system. The current design features a dual-strut rudder assembly
Figure 2, which increases the total surface area in the water. This enhancement improves directional stability and control,
particularly during high-speed runs and sharp turns. In PEP 2024, a single stinger rudder assembly was used. For PEP 2025, due
to the increased payload of 30–60 lbs, the design was upgraded to a dual-strut rudder system to maintain performance and
prevent washout during aggressive maneuvers. This configuration includes adjustable strut mounts for the drive cable, enabling
fine-tuning of motor angle for improved efficiency. Each rudder is also equipped with two water pickups, providing active
cooling to both ESCs and motors, which helps maintain consistent thermal management across the system. The drive cable is a
vital component in transmitting motor power efficiently. The current design uses two ¼ inch Hughey Drive Cables, chosen for
their ability to resist twisting under high torque. The increased diameter ensures consistent power delivery and reduces the risk of
failure under load. In the 2024 setup, a smaller drive cable was used, which led to a catastrophic failure during competition
Figure 3. As a result, the design was upgraded to a more robust ¼ in drive cable for 2025. The Hughey cable offers superior
strength and durability, significantly lowering the likelihood of mechanical failure and ensuring reliable operation under high
torque conditions. Figure 3: Failure from PEP 2024
The propeller, or prop, offers some of the most complexity and impact when it comes to drivetrain design and choice. Based
on the team’s research two categories of propeller variables yield the most influence while also being the most customizable.
These categories are propeller diameter and pitch or the theoretical distance a propeller would move forward in one revolution if
it were moving through a solid medium [4]. Propeller design from scratch is a highly cumbersome task, however, a large number
of options exist, as seen in Figure 4 that allow the team to sift through and optimize based on hull and drivetrain characteristics
The first prop variable that was optimized was the diameter. Using the calculations in Figure 5, an idealized size range was
found by incorporating the power needed based on hull length. To find the ideal pitch the calculations in Figure 6 were
performed. The equation used a variable boat speed, motor gear ratio (set as 1 since the team’s design is direct), engine rotation,
an assumed slip percentage (a type of pitch inefficiency), and a conversion constant. The calculation was repeated for an ideal no
slip condition as well an assumed slip condition. All results were averaged across a set of low to high speeds to achieve the most
balanced pitch for all possible conditions. Thus, two propeller designs were chosen from over a hundred options, one with the
original diameter (65mm), and a second based on the ideal pitch (4 in.) and an incrementally increased diameter (71mm) to
reduce cavitation while not interfering with the dual motor/propeller setup.
Figure 4: Section of Supplier’s Propeller Chart Figure 5: Propeller Diameter Calculation Figure 6: Propeller Pitch Calculations
Electrical and Power System Design
The RC boat’s original electrical system, based on a previous team’s design, had inefficiencies in weight distribution and
power management. It used ten batteries, adding excessive mass without proportional performance gains, and lacked adequate
circuit protection. To improve efficiency while meeting competition constraints, the new design optimizes power use, reduces
weight, and enhances safety. The battery count was reduced to eight, maintaining power output while lowering weight. A fuse
box and a waterproof 300A circuit breaker were added for protection. The improved system features eight 10,000 mAh, 6S-25C,
22.2V batteries in parallel, keeping voltage under the 55V limit. The propulsion system includes kV500 motors with neodymium
magnets, delivering up to 15,800W. The OM-300 AHV 300A RC Boat ESC ensures efficient motor control, while 6 AWG and 8
AWG wiring with XT90 and EC8 connectors handle high currents. For control, a Spektrum DX6C transmitter and SR515
receiver provide precise maneuverability. To reduce receiver load, hydraulic pumps (1000 cc/min flow rate) use an external
battery. These improvements enhance power management, reliability, and compliance with performance and safety requirements.
Payload Design
Research on payload systems for boats turned up minimal existing designs that were applicable. Full size systems for large
vessels were not feasible for the team’s boat size of 84 inches. For small model and RC boats, the most extensive systems simply
put weight on top of the hull meaning a fully original design was needed for the year’s weight requirements. Some military
applications exist but their specifics are not open source. To be in line with the direction of modern naval systems’ priority of
scalability and modularity, the payload system for the team’s boat focuses on flexible placement of multiple weights, secure lock
down during maneuvers, and an adaptable core set of parts that can be adjusted as needed. One of the largest challenges of the
payload system was overcoming the angled shape of our V-hull design. A method of cut and angled 2x4 wood beams was chosen
to level each side of the boat and create a stable foundation. This allowed for aluminum rails to be mounted giving way to the
use of heavy-duty locking rail carriages. Four carriages are used to create balanced and stable linear movement for each payload
while being able to lock in place when necessary. Multiple iterations of 3D printed risers are used to overcome spacing and
clearance issues such as with the locking mechanism of the carriage and the main drivetrain and battery elements in the center of
the boat. For the actual payload, 30lb ruck weights are used as they are an optional combination of a small form factor without
movement from a medium such as sandbags. Each weight is secured to the rest of the design through ¾ inch plywood, 3D
printed supports, ¼ inch bolts, and quick release nuts to ensure the payload’s stability when the boat is in motion. An overview
of the design is shown in Figure 7. Notably, the overall design permits two of the described systems giving the team the
flexibility to choose between carrying 30lbs or 60lbs. Figure 7: Payload System Overview
Hydromatic Addition Design
Turn fins, most commonly found on miniature race boats, are fixed past the transom of the craft to provide additional surface area
to create a counter-force when it makes turns. Many varying versions of turn fins exist, but few offer a size that the team deemed
optimal through a general observation of hull length to turn fin length ratios of about 1:11. To accommodate, the team 3D modeled
multiple sets of common turn fins in addition to creating an original design based on fish and rocket fins. The design combines the
low aspect and taper ratios (1:1.7) found in rocket fins and shark fins (sharks are optimal for comparison as they are more stiff than
other fish, resembling a boat better), with the higher ratios (1:7) found in wind sails. This shape mimics dorsal fins found in what
research has shown to be faster fish as well as the “shark fin” of F1 race cars of the past. To mount the turn fins a custom design
was created to permit the best range of motion of adjusting the fins’ angle. The trim tab design utilizes locking hinges that can be
set at any angle from 0 to 180 degrees. Sizing was determined by recommendations of one inch of span per foot of hull length.
Figure 8: Hydrodynamic Addition Overview
Custom Mounting Designs
A custom mount was designed to secure the stuffing tubes and house the circuit breakers Figure 9. This setup was chosen to
maximize internal space while also providing easy access to the circuit breakers in case they trip during operation. Additionally,
the mount keeps the stuffing tubes firmly in place, helping to minimize vibration and unwanted movement while the craft is
running.
Figure 9: Custom Mount for Drive Cables and ESC’s
To help optimize the boat weight and improve efficiency of the electrical system, custom battery mounts were modelled using
SOLIDWORKS then 3D printed, as shown in Figure 10. Two mounts were printed, each able to hold up to four batteries. Each
battery will be held in a separate slot and secured by a custom harness utilizing a velcro strip connected to a scaled belt buckle, as
shown in Figure 11. This harness system allows for quick installation and removal of each battery, which could be critical for
preserving integrity of various components or systems inside the boat. One slot in each set is angled and has a smaller slot
embossed into the angled end, allowing for the other security system to activate. This system is a spring lock mechanism located
inside the angled end of the battery slot base, as shown in Figure 12. A spring block connected to an external grip will be pushed
into the angled slot by two internal springs, which can be compressed via the external grip when removal is desired. Each set of
slots will be connected to a wood locking block underneath, which will link each set of four slots and act as a secondary form of
security simultaneously.
Figure 10: Overview of Battery Mount. Figure 11: Belt Buckle/Strip Harness System.
Figure 12: Spring Lock Mechanism. Hull
To provide extra visualization and a foundation for expected boat performance, hydrodynamic and vector analysis was
conducted. The hydrodynamic analysis of the boat hull was conducted first to visualize the benefit of hull strakes and gain a basic
understanding of what performance to expect at peak operational condition. A simplified version of the boat model was recreated
with and without strakes while water conditions were studied at the site of operation, shown in Figure 13 and 14. Preliminary
hydrodynamic diffraction was conducted before hydrodynamic responses were studied. The frequency of the wave movement
while moving was adjusted alongside the water speed to help visualize how the boat will react to the expected conditions. The
results of this hydrodynamic analysis were significant in estimating the performance of the boat when including the weight of the
payload alongside the internals. The hull studied without strakes was shown to drift to one side, with a longer simulation resulting
in the boat tipping. The hull with strakes included showed much better performance stability wise, with minimal drifting that
could easily be accounted for with trim settings. To further visualize and study the boat’s performance under operational
conditions, a multi-phase flow vector analysis was conducted. The analysis was conducted with the hull with strakes included
utilized in the previous analysis at the peak expected operational speed. The results of the simulation yielded promising results,
with a wake expected to pass around but not over the boat, which is expected to improve as planning is achieved. The vector field
of the expected wake is shown in Figure 15. The wake is also expected to keep the propeller submerged despite the amount of
water displaced, further contributing to the planning potential. Utilizing the built in characteristics calculator in ANSYS Fluent
post alongside material and weight data, the expected drag force was able to be determined, which is around 40 lb (177 N) when
travelling at 48 mph.
Figure 13: Simplified Hull w/o Strakes Figure 14: Simplified Hull With Strakes
Figure 15: Vector Field of Multi-Phase Flow Analysis
Drivetrain Analysis
The team plotted the thrust output of the motors across various speeds Figure 16 to better understand their performance
characteristics under different operating conditions. This visualization provides a clear representation of how thrust varies with

speed, enabling identification of the motor’s efficiency range and highlighting the speeds at which performance peaks or begins to taper off. By analyzing this data, the team was able to determine the optimal throttle settings that balance power consumption
with propulsion efficiency—particularly important when operating under payload conditions between 30–60 lbs. The resulting
thrust curve also informed decisions regarding battery selection and propeller choice, ensuring that the drivetrain operates within
its most effective range. Additionally, having access to this data allows for the simulation of different mission profiles and
provides insight into how the system will respond in real-world conditions, such as accelerating out of turns or maintaining high
speeds during straight-line sprints. Ultimately, this analysis is crucial for fine-tuning the craft to optimize both performance and
reliability.
Figure 16: Thrust - Speed Data Figure 17: Thrust - Speed Graph
Electrical and Power System Analysis
The redesigned electrical and power system significantly enhances the RC boat’s performance, efficiency, and reliability while
meeting all competition constraints. One of the most important improvements was the optimization of the battery configuration.
By reducing the battery count from ten to eight, the system achieves a more efficient power-to-weight ratio without
compromising performance. This adjustment lowers the overall mass of the boat, improving buoyancy and maneuverability while
maintaining sufficient power output. The parallel battery configuration ensures consistent voltage levels, providing stable power
delivery to the propulsion and auxiliary systems. A key consideration in the design was circuit protection. The inclusion of a
waterproof 300A circuit breaker and fuse box mitigates the risk of electrical failures, safeguarding both the components and
overall system integrity. This protection is essential given the high current demands of the propulsion system, which operates at
peak loads nearing 15,800W. Without adequate circuit protection, excessive current draw could lead to overheating, component
damage, or system shutdowns, all of which could jeopardize the boat’s performance during the competition. The selection of the
kV500 motors and OM-300 AHV, 300A ESC was based on a balance between power efficiency and control precision. The
motors, equipped with neodymium magnets, offer high torque and energy efficiency, enabling the boat to maintain optimal thrust
without unnecessary power losses. The ESC further enhances performance by regulating motor speed and ensuring smooth
acceleration and deceleration, critical for maintaining control over the boat during the 2-mile course. The use of 6 AWG and 8
AWG wiring minimizes resistive losses, preventing voltage drops that could otherwise impact motor efficiency and system
stability. Another critical improvement was the separation of the hydraulic pumps from the main power system by assigning
them an external battery source. This prevents excessive current draw from interfering with the propulsion system, reducing the
risk of power fluctuations that could impair maneuverability. The integration of the Spektrum DX6C transmitter and SR515
receiver provides precise control, allowing for accurate adjustments to steering and throttle inputs. These enhancements
collectively ensure the RC boat operates efficiently while maintaining the necessary power levels for propulsion and auxiliary

functions. To provide a clear representation of the electrical layout, a schematic diagram of the system is included below, Figures 18 and 19. This schematic illustrates the connections between the batteries, circuit protection elements, ESC, motors,
hydraulic pumps, and control components. Key aspects highlighted in the diagram include: Power Distribution, Circuit
Protection, Motor & ESC Connections, Control System.
Figure 18: Parallel Battery Schematic Figure 19: Main Electronic component Section
Overall, the redesigned electrical and power system successfully addresses the inefficiencies of the previous
iteration by optimizing power distribution, implementing robust circuit protection, and improving energy efficiency. These
improvements contribute to a more reliable and high-performing vessel capable of completing the 2-mile course within the
required 55-minute time frame while adhering to all competition constraints.
Payload Analysis
Given the need for reliability within the payload system an simulation based analysis of various the key structural components
was done in SolidWorks. Using a full 3D render allowed the team to pinpoint the most crucial elements of the design within a
greater visual context. The following simulations were completed by reducing a 30lb distributed load along the top surface:
deformation analysis, stress analysis, strain analysis, and a factor of safety (FOS) analysis shown in Figure 20. Since the 3D
model used to simulate the payload system was a 1:1 working digital version of what would become the actual system, accurate
material properties were compiled into the software to allow each component to be realistically depicted under load. The results
of the simulation yield a deformation range of 3.9x10 to 1.1x inches with the max occurring at the center of the plywood −32 10−4
support. The stress ranged from 1.2x10 to 8.6x psi with a section of the aluminum rails under most force per area. The −3 101
strain results ranged from 3.9x10 to 1.7x with the highest amounts occurring at the edges of the large 3D printed risers. −9 10−5
To better contextualize these results the FOS results offer the most insight. With a range of 4.6x10 to 8.8x , most of the 1
system lay within the lower end of the FOS, however, this value is still significantly large and permitted the team to move
forward with the design with greater confidence. Figure 20: Structural Analysis via Solidworks
Propeller Analysis
To visualize and confirm the performance improvements of larger propellers, simulation utilizing ANSYS Fluent was
conducted. The study was dedicated to comparing the set of 2.5 inch diameter propellers with a 3.5 inch pitch to an upgraded 2.7
inch diameter set of propellers with a 4.32 inch pitch. The main point of focus for each simulation was the amount of thrust and
torque each propeller can output. Pressure contours and water velocity vector fields were also synthesized for supporting
analysis. These characteristics were determined to be the most relevant points of study due to their potential impact on the boat
throughout operation. Both propellers will experience 11,000 RPM at 40 mph to simulate close to maximum expected operational
conditions, with all movement other than rotation on the Z axis locked. Due to the focus on geometry, material properties will not
be relevant throughout this study despite being accurately assigned. Initial research of the impact of an increased diameter and
pitch showed that the increased diameter will have a greater thrust and torque but experience greater drag, while the increased
pitch would allow for a higher top speed at the cost of a slower acceleration. The results of the study yielded promising
results, with the 2.7 in diameter propeller demonstrating an average thrust of around 875 N (~196 lbf) after achieving stable
operation 1 second after startup, both of which are shown on Figure 21. The 2.7 in propeller achieved an average torque of
around 12 Nm (~106 in-lb), shown in Figure 22. The 2.5 in propeller yielded expected results, with an average thrust of around
462.5 N (~104 lbf) after reaching stability half a second after startup, as shown in Figure 23. The 2.5 in propeller achieved an
average torque of around 8 Nm (~70 in-lb) after reaching stability in a similar time frame to the thrust graph as shown in Figure
24. Each force and torque graph pair share a very similar curve due to the thrust and torque applied being proportional to each
other. These simulations confirm the validity of the initial research, as the 2.7 in propeller had greater amount of thrust and torque
compared to the 2.5 in propeller while experiencing a slower acceleration to stability by half a second. Water velocity vector
profiles and pressure contours were also synthesized for study. Figures 25 and 26 show the face and back pressure contours for
the 2.5 in propeller, with the back side of the propeller being of note due to the presence of multiple smaller low pressure zones
having a high potential to cause cavitation during physical operation. Figures 27 and 28 show the face and back pressure
contours for the 2.7 in propeller, which show more consistent pressure zones. These pressure zones being more consistent
translates to less cavitation at the operational RPM, solidifying the 2.7 in diameter propeller as beneficial and necessary for
optimal operation. Figures 29 and 30 show the water velocity vector profiles for the 2.5 and 2.7 inch propellers respectively. The
water movement around the 2.5 in propeller is faster in comparison to the 2.7 in propeller, which confirms that a smaller diameter
propeller will be faster and produce less drag than a larger diameter propeller, but will reduce the amount of torque output.
Figure 21: 2.7 in Diameter Propeller Thrust Graph Figure 22: 2.7 in Diameter Propeller Torque Graph
Figure 23: 2.5 in Diameter Propeller Thrust Graph Figure 24: 2.5 in Diameter Propeller Torque Graph
Figure 25: face side pressure contour of 2.5 in Prop Figure 26: back side pressure contour of 2.5 in Prop

Figure 27: face side pressure contour of 2.7 in Prop Figure 28: back side pressure contour of 2.7 in Prop Figure 29: Water Velocity Vector Field of 2.5 in Propeller Figure 30: Water Velocity Vector Field of 2.7 in Propeller
Build & Fabrication
Drivetrain
The majority of the build and fabrication phase of this project was focused on the drivetrain. The first step was mounting the
rudder, as its position determined the alignment and fitment of the remaining components. Next, the team fiberglassed wood
stringers into the hull, providing a rigid and secure base for all components without needing to drill directly into the boat itself.
Following that, the motors were mounted to the stingers using custom CNC-machined aluminum mounts. They were set at a
5-degree downward angle to help reduce cavitation and ensure efficient power transmission Figure 1. We then bent and installed
the stuffing tubes using our custom mount. The tubes were shaped in an S-curve to help reduce vibration from the flexible drive
shaft. Final steps included installing Teflon washers to minimize friction between the struts and props. The drive cables were
greased, inserted through the stuffing tubes, and secured to the motors. Lastly, the props were attached and locked in place using
nylon locking nuts.
Electrical and Power System
During the building and fabrication of the unmanned boat, the placement of electronic components was carefully determined
after implementing the drivetrain, which occupied a significant amount of space near the transom. With the batteries positioned at
the nose of the boat to aid in weight distribution, the remaining electronics had to be rearranged to fit efficiently within the
available space. As a result, the ESC was positioned directly underneath the motor, while the circuit breaker was mounted on
custom-made stuffing tube mounts. These placement decisions were influenced by several critical factors, including balance, heat
dissipation, and accessibility for maintenance. Placing the ESC under the motor minimized wiring complexity by reducing the
length of connections between key components, which helped optimize power delivery and system efficiency. Additionally, this
location provided adequate airflow to help dissipate heat generated during operation, preventing potential overheating issues. The
circuit breaker was strategically mounted on the stuffing tube mounts to ensure it remained secure while also being easily
accessible for maintenance and troubleshooting. This placement facilitated quick power isolation if needed, enhancing both
safety and ease of operation. Overall, these design choices allowed for an efficient, well-organized layout that balanced
performance, thermal management, and serviceability within the spatial constraints of the vessel. Payload
The foundation of the payload system hindered upon the size, space, and geometry of the hull. Internal measurements were
taken to set a baseline for design and fabrication. Most importantly, each side of the hull was measured which produced unique
angles due. While only minimally different with the left side being 15 degrees and the right being 18 degrees, accounting for this
difference was critical for the rest of the design. This was displayed most critically in the wood supports that used 2x4 studs cut
using a table saw into right triangles with each of aforementioned angles thus leveling each side. The supports were then
fiberglassed into the hull to create a high-strength base. The even surface created by the supports allows the rail system to
operate as smoothly as possible. Said rail system is mounted using M5 bolts/screws/nuts. It was decided to have the screws
come from the bottom of the wood support to prevent them from being easily ripped out. This decision required countersunk
holes to keep the critical angle alignment. Additionally, the first set of 3D printed risers were created to allow the rails to sit
higher above the wood allowing the locking mechanism of the rail carriage to operate. The second set of risers were made larger
and more robust to copacetically fit with the rail carriages while supporting the load and providing clearance above the drivetrain
and electrical systems. M4 screws/nuts were used to fix these items together. The main ¾ inch plywood support was cut to the
largest size that could fit inside the access point of the hull to maximize the distribution of the load. Mounting holes were then
drilled along a calculated pattern that permitted the plywood to be fixed to the larger rise supports. Additional supports for the
payload were 3D printed to lock the ruck weight in place and prevent displacements through multiple degrees of motion. These
elements were then assembled with ¼ inch bolts/nuts to ensure strength and stability. A ¼ inch plywood sheet was then used as a
lid with the same hole pattern. The design intentionally let the bolts show above the lit which permits the use of specially quick
release, push-button ¼ inch nuts to be used for locking the weight in.
Custom Mounting
Design of the custom battery mount needed to take the boat stringers and boat geometry into account, which was done through
measurements taken before design was initiated. The critical measurements taken were the distance between the stringers (insert
here) and an internal angle of 20 degrees inside the boat. The first step to assembly was gluing the mounting bases together,
which was done using Weld-On 16 acrylic cement due to the nature of its chemical bond providing unmatched strength. At the
same time, the wood locking base was cut from stock wood and glued together with wood glue. After the bonding time had
passed, the mounting base and wood locking base was tested to confirm correct sizing. The battery slot assemblies were then
assembled as parts were delivered, utilizing a plastic hinge and a velcro strip connected to the belt clip. The clip and harness base
were both secured to each slot with 8 total M4x8 screws. Once the mounting slots and wood locking base are complete, they will
be glued together with a thin coat of a universal adhesive. Before the mounting base is glued onto a wood base inside the boat,
the spring lock system will be assembled with Weld-On 16. Epoxy resin will be used to glue the mounting base to the wood base,
which will then be attached to the boat internally in a similar fashion.
Hydrodynamic Additions
Turnfins and trimtabs will be 3D printed for testing. An infill of 50% or greater will be used to provide the greatest strength
and reliability. Once the final designs are determined, the turn fins and trimtabs will be CNC machined out of an aluminum alloy
metal. The turn fins and trim tabs will be mounted to the rear of the craft. Mounting holes will be drilled to allow M4 screws to
pass through, and the components will be secured using nylon locking nuts. To ensure a watertight seal and prevent any leaks,
3M marine sealant will be applied around the mounting points during installation. The actual additions will be 3D printed at high
infill percentages for the highest quality results. Testing
A series of tests will be conducted to verify the boat’s seaworthiness, endurance, and overall performance. Testing will take
place at either Swan Lake or Robious Landing Park, both locations provide calm waters and sufficient space for full-capacity
operation. The first test will involve placing the boat in the water to check for leaks and ensure all systems are functioning
correctly, including the motors, ESCs, rudder, and water pumps. A force gauge will be attached to measure thrust at various
throttle levels.The second test will assess the boat’s endurance by verifying it can travel 2 miles without any added payload. The
third and fourth tests will evaluate performance under load: first with a 30-pound payload, then with a 60-pound payload, each
over a 2-mile course. Additional tests will focus on maneuverability and handling to familiarize the team with boat operation and
to identify and address any potential issues prior to competition.
Risk
Drivetrain
For the motors, the primary risk lies in power consumption. Due to their high-performance nature, they draw significant
power, which could lead to rapid battery drain. To mitigate this, we plan to test various throttle settings and optimize our battery
usage accordingly. Additionally, we aim to implement battery telemetry for real-time voltage monitoring to prevent unexpected
power loss during operation. For the rudder, the main concern is increased drag. Since we are using a dual rudder setup, there is
more surface area in the water, which slightly increases resistance. However, given the high thrust output from the motors, this
additional drag is minimal and considered negligible in terms of overall performance. The risk associated with the drive shaft is
excessive friction and mechanical stress, which could lead to failure. To address this, we will follow a strict maintenance
routine—cleaning and drying the shaft after each use and applying fresh grease before every run to ensure smooth operation and
longevity. For the props, the risk is potential loosening or imbalance during operation. To prevent this, we use nylon locking nuts
to secure the props and inspect them regularly for wear or damage. Ensuring they are properly torqued and balanced helps
maintain efficiency and avoid mechanical issues at high speeds.
Electrical and Power System
To address the risks associated with the electrical components and power systems, several design strategies and preventative
measures were implemented to enhance the safety, reliability, and performance of the unmanned boat. One of the primary
