concerns was heat buildup due to the ESC’s placement directly underneath the motor. To mitigate this, adequate ventilation was
ensured by allowing sufficient airflow around the ESC and motor, enabling natural heat dissipation. Additionally, a heat sink was
installed on the ESC to improve thermal regulation and prevent overheating during extended operation. The circuit breaker’s
location on custom-made stuffing tube mounts initially posed a risk of mechanical stress and vibrations from the drivetrain,
which could lead to unintentional tripping or premature wear. To counter this, vibration-dampening materials were integrated into
the mounting system, reducing excessive movement and preventing accidental breaker trips. The breaker was also strategically
positioned to remain easily accessible for maintenance while being securely fastened to prevent disconnections due to mechanical
strain. Another potential risk was electromagnetic interference (EMI) affecting signal integrity due to the proximity of
high-current components. To resolve this, shielded cables were used for critical wiring, particularly for data and control lines,
while power cables were routed separately to minimize interference. Additionally, secure cable management techniques,
including zip ties and protective tubing, were employed to prevent accidental disconnections, wire fatigue, or damage from
vibrations. By implementing these mitigation strategies, the risks associated with the electrical and power systems were
effectively reduced, ensuring stable performance, reliability, and longevity of the unmanned boat’s electrical components. Payload
The payload presents a number of risks, most prominently from unwanted displacements and structural failure. Having a
movable payload is critical for accessing other elements and testing the optimal position for operation. Since a moveable payload
is so critical for the design, the application of locking rail carriages to fix the payload in place was essential in addressing any
concerns. The carriages are also rated to withstand a large amount of force from pitching, yawing, and rolling motions,
especially when used congruently in multiples. Material selection and geometric design was done in a fashion that combined
desirable traits and distributed loads over larger areas while resisting deformation. The load simulations run helped confirm that
the team adequately addressed any risk related to the loads. As was also mentioned above, 3D printing allowed many elements to
be iterated upon reducing the risk of impeding on other critical components. The strategic use of push-button quick-release nuts
also gives the team a faster way to prepare the payload during the five minutes allowed after the weight-in stage. This reduces
the risk of the team being penalized for a time violation without compromising structural integrity.
Custom Mounting
The primary risk associated with the battery mounting system is structural failure. Fatigue and stress failure concerns are
present throughout the system but the most critical is fatigue failure in the belt clip. The belt clip system is capable of supporting
the battery when the full weight of the battery is placed on it, but over multiple unlocking and locking cycles the belt clip prongs
will begin to experience plastic deformation, loosening the clip until it could potentially be shaken free or snap from overuse.
This potential failure point Is alleviated by increasing the size of the belt clip system, increasing the yield strength of the prongs
and allowing for longer continued use. Another potential point of failure is stress failure of the wood base holding the mounting
system inside the boat. Due to the weight of the batteries on the mount there is potential for either the wood base to snap, or the
epoxy resin to fail. If time permits, a successful solution would involve creating a vertical support below the base, utilizing the
bottom of the boat to alleviate the stress the wood base would experience.
Hydrodynamic Additions
The primary risk of the hydrodynamic additions is structural failure. Most pre-made versions of these designs use CNC
technology. This is an option that the current team will keep on the table and pass on to future teams. However, given the current
set of time and monetary constraints, 3D printing offers the most viable solution. As mentioned in the fabrication section, high
infill rates will increase the density of the prints ensuring a more durable construction. Furthermore, a cross-compatible
mounting design for the original trim tabs will be used to allow them to be interchangeable with the procured version, limiting the
risk of unnecessary hull patching. A secondary risk associated with the trim tabs and turn fins is improper alignment or
installation, which can lead to handling instability or inefficient hydrodynamics. If the trim tabs are not correctly leveled, the craft
may experience uneven lift or porpoising at high speeds. Similarly, misaligned turn fins can cause unpredictable turning behavior
or increased drag. To mitigate these risks, precise measurement and alignment will be performed during installation, and all
hardware will be securely fastened using nylon locking nuts and marine sealant to prevent shifting during operation. Regular
inspections will be conducted to ensure components remain tight and properly positioned after each run. Another potential risk is
water leakage through the mounting holes; this will be addressed by applying 3M marine-grade sealant around all screw holes to
maintain watertight integrity.Citations
